title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text: This comparison focuses on the trade-offs between direct estimation, area-level SAE, unit-level SAE models, with and without poststratification.

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text:
1 Estimate Scale and Smoothing
The distribution and rank plots compare the spread of MSOA-year estimates across methods, while the maps compare the local pattern of estimated frequent cycling.

Direct estimates retain the most cell-level variation. Model-based estimates are smoother because they borrow strength across areas, years, predictors, or poststratification cells. The area-level FH model is anchored by the direct estimates, so weak direct evidence can still influence the modelled results. The lower mean estimate in 2023 is consistent with weaker direct-estimate input in that wave, possibly due to smaller sample sizes.
Differences between the two unit-level models are more subtle because they use similar models and spatio-temporal structure. Their main difference is the aggregation step: the poststratified model averages predictions over age-sex-car population cells, while the area-summary model substitutes MSOA-level predictor summaries. Poststratification better aligns predictions with the target population composition; area-summary substitution is more approximate and does not itself correct survey selection bias.

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text:
2 Uncertainty CI Width
Interval width shows the precision gained or lost by each method. Direct-estimate widths reflect sampling variance, while model-based widths reflect posterior uncertainty after borrowing strength across areas, years, or predictors.

title: Model diagnostics and comparison
text:
3 Residual Area Effects
The unstructured area-effect maps show where the fitted models allocate remaining area-level variation after the fixed effects and temporal and spatial structure are considered.

title: Unit-level SAE model with area summaries
text:
Theory in brief



Unit-level SAE models the individual outcome before aggregating predictions to area-time estimates. For a continuous outcome, the unit-level model can be written as:

Y_{ijt}
=
\alpha + \mathbf{x}_{ijt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + v_t + \epsilon_{ijt}.

Here, \mathbf{x}_{ijt} contains unit-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, v_t is a time effect, and \epsilon_{ijt} is residual error. For a binary outcome, the model predicts the probability that Y_{ijt}=1. Population summaries of the predictors \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{jt} are substituted into the fitted unit-level model:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j, t, \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{jt}).

title: Unit-level SAE model with area summaries
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Unit-level SAE models survey microdata directly instead of starting from pre-aggregated direct estimates, which helps when direct estimates are too sparse or unstable to provide reliable modelling inputs. Here, the binary frequent-cycling indicator freq_cyclist is modelled from the survey microdata using temporal and spatial random effects, with unit-level age, sex, and caraccess added across model specifications.
This method follows the classic Battese–Harter–Fuller (BHF) unit-level SAE model, extended here through a generalised mixed model so it can be used with both continuous and binary outcomes. The individual outcome is modelled using predictors present in the survey microdata, then evaluated using MSOA-level summaries of those predictors. Here, those summaries are extracted from ONS UK Census 2021 to produce the final MSOA-year estimates. This reduces reliance on unstable or missing direct estimates, but it assumes the area summaries of age, sex, and caraccess adequately represent the target population composition in each MSOA-year cell.






Continuous and binary outcomes



For continuous outcomes, area-level predictor summaries can be substituted into the fitted model to obtain an area-level prediction, since predicting at the average predictor values gives the same result as averaging predictions over individuals.
For binary outcomes such as freq_cyclist, the target is the population proportion in the area, which is best estimated by averaging predicted probabilities over the area population. Substituting area-level summaries into the model is only an approximation to that population average.

2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit binomial unit-level models to the survey microdata, then use them to predict area-time means. We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:

Name
Specifications




M1

M2
+Demographic

M3

m1_formula <- freq_cyclist ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  age +
  female
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  caraccess
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)


fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)

control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.

title: Unit-level SAE model with area summaries
section: 3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
text:
3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
The aggregation step uses posterior draws from the selected INLA fit to produce unit-level SAE estimates for each MSOA-year cell. We first sample from the posterior and extract the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect. We then rebuild the fitted model for every MSOA-year aggregation row and summarise the resulting draws.






Note



Each posterior draw stores the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect together in INLA’s latent vector. Fixed effects are labelled as term:1, while random effects are labelled as effect:index.



# Draw 300 posterior samples from the selected fit.
set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = bhf_selected_fit
)

# Fixed-effect draw matrix
fixed_terms <- rownames(bhf_selected_fit$summary.fixed)
fixed_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"), 1]),
    fixed_terms
  )
})

# Area-effect draw matrix
area_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids), 1]),
    area_ids
  )
})

# Time-effect draw matrix
time_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids), 1]),
    time_ids
  )
})

Each posterior draw is evaluated over the MSOA-year aggregation frame.

prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ age + female + caraccess,
  data = aggregation_data
)[, fixed_terms, drop = FALSE]

prediction_draws <- sapply(seq_along(posterior_draws), \(draw_id) {
  log_odds <- as.numeric(prediction_matrix %*% fixed_draws[, draw_id]) +
    area_draws[as.character(aggregation_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    time_draws[as.character(aggregation_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  plogis(log_odds) # For binomial model
})

The matrix prediction_draws has one MSOA-year estimate per row and one posterior draw per column. Posterior means, variances, and 95% credible intervals are computed directly from this draw matrix.

final_bhf_results <- aggregation_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id) |>
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      bhf_estimate = rowMeans(prediction_draws),
      bhf_variance = apply(prediction_draws, 1, var),
      bhf_lower = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      bhf_upper = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    bhf_ci_width = bhf_upper - bhf_lower
  )

Although unit-level modelling can stabilise estimates where direct estimates are weak, aggregation using area-level predictor summaries still relies on strong assumptions about population composition. Representing age, sex, and car access using mean adult age, the adult female share, and the adult share with car access can conceal important differences in their joint distribution. Two areas may have similar marginal summaries but very different age–sex–car compositions, leading to similar model-based estimates even when cycling behaviour differs across particular population groups.
This limitation is especially important for a binary outcome modelled using a logistic model (i.e., family = "binomial"). The target is the population-average predicted probability, but substituting area-level predictor summaries estimates the probability at the average predictor values:

\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha + \mathbf{x}_{i}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta})
\neq
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha + \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta}).

A poststratification table addresses this limitation by providing population counts for the joint combinations of the relevant predictors. This is the logic of multilevel regression with poststratification (MRP): predict the outcome for each population cell, then aggregate the cell predictions using the corresponding population counts so that the final estimate reflects the composition of the target population.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The analysis uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on three waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW): 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
The raw survey geography and stratification variable is Local Authority, while the estimation domain here is MSOA. The cleaned survey file therefore assigns each respondent to a synthetic MSOA within their Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. The resulting MSOA estimates should not be interpreted as substantive findings about individual places.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution. The synthetic MSOA assignment supports MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and unit-level SAE with poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



Survey period labels use their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. Here, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.
The target estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025






2.2 Preparing the Survey Indicator and Weight
The estimand is the proportion of the target population who cycle frequently. We therefore code the survey response as a binary indicator, freq_cyclist, because the average of a binary indicator gives the estimated prevalence. freq_cyclist is coded from AtFrqBke, the active-travel frequency question for cycling:

1: AtFrqBke is 1 or 2, meaning at least several times a week
0: less frequent cycling or never cycling
NA: missing, ineligible, or not asked

For each survey respondent, we also need a design weight, which adjusts the sample so that weighted estimates better represent the target population. Since the survey question was administered to all respondents during some survey periods and subsampled in others, the corresponding weight variable selection rule is as follows:

Use SampleTravelWeight in survey waves where this question was asked to a subsample and the corresponding weight for this module exists,
Use SampleAdultWeight in survey waves where this question was asked to the main sample.

The survey design may include stratum, which records the sampling group each respondent belongs to. Including it helps the variance calculation reflect how the sample was drawn, if not randomised.

title: Direct estimation
text:
Theory in brief



For an area-time cell (j,t), the target is a population mean or proportion:

\mu_{jt} = \frac{1}{N_{jt}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{jt}} y_{ijt}.

If sampled unit i has inclusion probability \pi_{ijt} and design weight w_{ijt}=1/\pi_{ijt}, the Horvitz–Thompson ratio estimator gives the design-weighted direct estimate:

\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} =
\frac{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt} y_{ijt}}
{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt}}.

title: Direct estimation
text:
3 Assess precision and coverage
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because it makes three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and MSOAs, leaving some area-time cells with much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimates over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves, which may reflect real behavioural change or sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, small samples can contain only one response value, producing zero or unrealistically low variances.










Sparse and uneven survey coverage limits how far direct estimates can be used on their own. At the target MSOA-year scale, many estimates are unstable or unavailable, so the next step is to use model-based SAE methods that borrow strength across areas, years, and auxiliary predictors.
Two model-based options follow:

Area-level SAE models stabilise direct area estimates using sampling variances to control how much weight each direct estimate receives.
Unit-level SAE models estimate the individual outcome from survey microdata and aggregate predictions to target area-years.

title: Area-level SAE model
text:
Theory in brief



The area-level model treats each direct estimate hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} as a noisy observation of a true estimate \mu_{jt}:

\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} \mid \mu_{jt}
&\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{jt}, \psi_{jt}), \\
\mu_{jt}
&= \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + v_t.
\end{aligned}

Here, \psi_{jt} is the direct-estimation sampling variance, \mathbf{x}_{jt} contains area-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model produces the area-time estimate by combining the direct estimate, its sampling variance, and the model prediction:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu_{jt} \mid \hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt}, \psi_{jt}, \mathbf{x}_{jt}).

title: Area-level SAE model
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal and spatial effect


M2
+AvgAge
M1 plus mean adult age


M3
+PopdensCaraccess
M2 plus population density and share of adults with car access



The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.







Temporal model
Description




rw1
First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods.


rw2
Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series.


ar1
Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years.










Spatial model
Description




besag
Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation.


bym2
Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, phi, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured.



With only three survey years, rw1 is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, bym2 is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_age_adult_mean
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_pop_density +
  scaled_caraccess_adult_share
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +AvgAge" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +PopdensCaraccess" = m3_formula
)


fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When fitting area-level SAE models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
scale passes the inverse sampling variance to INLA, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
control.family fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.



Model fit is compared with WAIC (Widely Applicable Information Criterion), a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA. Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

4.2 Adding Temporal and Spatial Effects
The selected area-level model estimates hyperparameters for the temporal and spatial random effects. These parameters show how much residual variation remains after accounting for the fixed-effect predictors and sampling variances, and how that remaining variation is structured across time and space.

tau is the precision of a random effect, or the inverse of its variance. Higher precision means less residual variation in that component. A higher temporal tau than spatial indicates a smoother time pattern with smaller differences between neighbouring survey years than between MSOAs. The temporal random effect keeps wave-to-wave differences explicit instead of pooling the three waves into one period.
phi is the BYM2 mixing parameter for the area random effect. It describes how much of that residual area effect is spatially structured. A lower phi here (less than 0.5) means the remaining area differences are mostly local and less strongly explained by adjacency. This can also be due to sparse direct estimates in many areas, which give the model less reliable area-level evidence for learning a coherent spatial pattern.

title: Unit-level SAE model with poststratification
text:
Theory in brief



Unit-level SAE models the individual outcome before aggregating predictions to area-time estimates. For a continuous outcome, the unit-level model can be written as:

Y_{ijt}
=
\alpha + \mathbf{x}_{ijt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + v_t + \epsilon_{ijt}.

Here, \mathbf{x}_{ijt} contains unit-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, v_t is a time effect, and \epsilon_{ijt} is residual error. For a binary outcome, the model predicts the probability that Y_{ijt}=1. The fitted model is first evaluated for each population cell c:

\hat{\mu}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j, t, \mathbf{x}_{jtc}).

The final area-time estimate is the population-weighted average of those cell predictions:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\mu}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}},

where N_{jtc} is the population count for cell c in area j and time t.

title: Unit-level SAE model with poststratification
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Unit-level SAE with poststratification combines an outcome model fitted to survey microdata with a poststratification table describing the target population. This is the core structure of Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP): model predictions are averaged over population cells. For this estimand, we model the binary frequent-cycling indicator freq_cyclist using age_band, sex, caraccess, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for each age_band x sex x caraccess population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
Here, the poststratification table is sourced from ONS UK Census 2021, giving the 2021 population count for each age_band x sex x caraccess cell in each MSOA. For the 2023 and 2025 estimands, the model can still estimate different area-time outcomes through the temporal and spatial terms, but the poststratification weights are held fixed. This assumes that local demographic and car-access composition does not change across the survey years. In other words, N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021} for all three waves.

title: Unit-level SAE model with poststratification
text:
3 Poststratification with posterior draws
As with the previous model-based methods, the final MSOA-year estimates are obtained by aggregating predictions across posterior draws. The key difference is that the unit-level model is fitted to survey microdata, so its predictions can still reflect the composition of the survey sample instead of the real-world population if left unadjusted as done in the previous method. Poststratification addresses this by evaluating the fitted model over known population groups and reweighting those predictions by population counts, so the final estimates are aligned with the target population structure.





Posterior draws from the selected INLA fit produce MSOA-year estimates. Each draw provides fixed effects, spatial area effects, and temporal effects. The fitted model is evaluated over every age_band x sex x caraccess population cell, transformed to the response scale, weighted by pop_count, and summarised as MSOA-year draws.






Note



Each posterior draw stores the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect together in INLA’s latent vector. Fixed effects are labelled as term:1, while random effects are labelled as effect:index.



set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = mrp_final_fit
)

# Fixed-effect draw matrix
fixed_terms <- rownames(mrp_final_fit$summary.fixed)
fixed_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"), 1]),
    fixed_terms
  )
})

# Area-effect draw matrix
area_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids), 1]),
    area_ids
  )
})

# Time-effect draw matrix
time_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids), 1]),
    time_ids
  )
})

Each posterior draw is evaluated over every poststratification cell. The cell predictions are then weighted by population count and aggregated within each MSOA-year.

# Rebuild fitted model for each cell
prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ age_band + sex + caraccess,
  data = poststrat_data
)[, fixed_terms, drop = FALSE]

cell_draws <- sapply(seq_along(posterior_draws), \(draw_id) {
  cell_log_odds <- as.numeric(prediction_matrix %*% fixed_draws[, draw_id]) +
    area_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    time_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  plogis(cell_log_odds) # For binomial model
})

# Aggregate and apply poststrat weight for each area-time
area_year_id <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")

aggregate_draws <- function(draw_matrix, weights, group) {
  weighted_sums <- rowsum(draw_matrix * weights, group = group, reorder = FALSE)
  population_totals <- rowsum(weights, group = group, reorder = FALSE)
  weighted_sums / as.numeric(population_totals)
}

prediction_draws <- aggregate_draws(
  draw_matrix = cell_draws,
  weights = poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id
)

The matrix prediction_draws has one MSOA-year estimate per row and one posterior draw per column. Posterior means, variances, and 95% credible intervals are computed directly from this draw matrix.

  separate(area_year_id, into = c("area_id", "time_id"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE) |>

      mrp_variance = apply(prediction_draws, 1, var),
      mrp_lower = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      mrp_upper = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    mrp_ci_width = mrp_upper - mrp_lower
  )

In the modelling step, the model specification uses age_band and sex as the poststratification-cell predictors, and adds the contextual area predictors directly as fixed effect terms.

shallow_formula <- freq_cyclist ~
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  age_band +
  sex +
  pop_density +
  caraccess_adult_share

shallow_context_fit <- inla(
  formula = shallow_formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = 1,
  data = shallow_model_data,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
)

The WAIC comparison suggests that contextual predictors add less to model performance than the richer specification with the unit-level car-access predictor. When survey microdata and poststratification data are available at compatible predictor grains, the richer specification is preferred.

# Posterior draws
set.seed(101)
shallow_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = shallow_context_fit
)

shallow_fixed_terms <- rownames(shallow_context_fit$summary.fixed)
shallow_fixed_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0(shallow_fixed_terms, ":1"), 1]),
    shallow_fixed_terms
  )
})

shallow_area_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids), 1]),
    area_ids
  )
})

shallow_time_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids), 1]),
    time_ids
  )
})

# Predict
shallow_prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ age_band + sex + pop_density + caraccess_adult_share,
  data = shallow_poststrat_data
)[, shallow_fixed_terms, drop = FALSE]

shallow_cell_draws <- sapply(seq_along(shallow_draws), \(draw_id) {
  shallow_cell_log_odds <- as.numeric(
    shallow_prediction_matrix %*% shallow_fixed_draws[, draw_id]
  ) +
    shallow_area_draws[as.character(shallow_poststrat_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    shallow_time_draws[as.character(shallow_poststrat_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  plogis(shallow_cell_log_odds)
})

# Weight (poststrat)
shallow_area_year_id <- paste(
  shallow_poststrat_data$area_id,
  shallow_poststrat_data$time_id,
  sep = "__"
)

shallow_prediction_draws <- aggregate_draws(
  draw_matrix = shallow_cell_draws,
  weights = shallow_poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = shallow_area_year_id
)

# Results
shallow_mrp_results <- tibble(area_year_id = rownames(shallow_prediction_draws)) |>
  separate(area_year_id, into = c("area_id", "time_id"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE) |>
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      shallow_mrp_estimate = rowMeans(shallow_prediction_draws),
      shallow_mrp_variance = apply(shallow_prediction_draws, 1, var),
      shallow_mrp_lower = apply(shallow_prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      shallow_mrp_upper = apply(shallow_prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shallow_mrp_ci_width = shallow_mrp_upper - shallow_mrp_lower
  )
